Kenilworth.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of central Warwickshire
s1loc: Kenilworth anchors its visitor economy on Kenilworth Castle, the English Heritage medieval fortress and Elizabethan palace once home to Robert Dudley, with its great Norman keep, John of Gaunt's Great Hall, the gatehouse and the recreated Elizabethan Garden where Queen Elizabeth the First once walked. The sandstone ruins and the wider Tiltyard draw heritage day-trippers from across the Midlands through the warmer season, with the famous castle fireworks a marquee autumn date.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Abbey Fields, the green heart of the town with its grassy slopes, wildflower meadows, lake, duck-feeding platform, playgrounds, tennis courts and outdoor swimming pool beside the Abbey ruins. Crackley Woods, a Warwickshire Wildlife Trust nature reserve of ancient trees, meadows and streams north of the centre, plus walking with alpacas at Faerie Tale Farm, give families and activity operators a steady outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture run through St Nicholas Church, the Grade I medieval parish church in Abbey Fields whose ornate West door was built from Abbey stone by Robert Dudley to impress the Queen, and the Norman and Gothic ruins of the Abbey of St Mary the Virgin with its Abbey Museum. The Virgins and Castle, the town's oldest inn traced to 1563, and the Clarendon Arms at Castle Hill carry the events calendar through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, inn and guesthouse trade serving the Warwickshire visitor area, with a guide scene built on castle, abbey and heritage-trail tours, and Stoneleigh Abbey with its Jane Austen connections a short drive away. Kenilworth station runs trains toward Coventry and Leamington Spa, while the A46 and the wider Heart of Warwickshire draw weekend visitors out from Leamington Spa, Warwick and Coventry across the season.

Buxton.region: Buxton and the Derbyshire Peak District
Buxton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Peak District spa town
s1loc: Buxton, the Roman spa of Aquae Arnemetiae and one of the joint-highest market towns in England, anchors its visitor economy on the Crescent, the Georgian masterpiece built for the fifth Duke of Devonshire and reborn as a thermal spa hotel above St Ann's Well. The Devonshire Dome, one of the largest unsupported domes in Europe and now part of the University of Derby campus, and the elegant streets above the Slopes draw visitors across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the Pavilion Gardens, twenty-three acres of Victorian landscaped grounds laid out in the 1870s with lakes, a bandstand, a miniature railway and the glasshouse Octagon. Poole's Cavern and Buxton Country Park add a spectacular show cave and the Go Ape treetop course at Grin Low, while the surrounding moors of the Peak District National Park give activity operators and walkers a strong outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture run through the Buxton Opera House, the Grade II listed Edwardian theatre designed by Frank Matcham in 1903 and restored in 2001, home to the internationally renowned Buxton International Festival of opera, music and books each summer. The Buxton Museum and Art Gallery, the Fringe festival and the events calendar at the Pavilion Arts Centre carry visitors through the year in this Derbyshire dales town.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, inn and guesthouse trade led by the restored Crescent and the town's Victorian and Georgian houses, with a guide scene built on cavern, spa and Peak District walking tours. Buxton station runs direct trains to Manchester Piccadilly, while the A6, A53 and A515 carry day-trippers out toward the Goyt Valley, the High Peak and the towns of Glossop, Macclesfield and Chesterfield across the season.
Buxton.kit_loc: across the town's gardens, caverns and visitor sites

Market Harborough.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south Leicestershire
s1loc: Market Harborough anchors its visitor economy on St Dionysius Church, the Grade I medieval parish church whose 152-foot Decorated Gothic spire rises dramatically from the pavement over the High Street, with the timber-framed Old Grammar School of 1614 standing on its pillars beneath. The town where Charles the First billeted troops before the Battle of Naseby in 1645 draws heritage visitors and market-day crowds across the warmer season in this elegant Leicestershire market town.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the water at Union Wharf, the restored basin at the head of the Grand Union Canal's Market Harborough Arm, where red-brick warehouses, day-boat hire and a traffic-free towpath lead five and a half miles to Foxton Locks, the finest staircase-lock flight in the country. Walking, cycling, fishing and boat trips along the arm give families and activity operators a steady outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Harborough Museum, set in the former Symington corset factory and home to the internationally important Hallaton Treasure of over five thousand Roman coins, a gold helmet and the Symington fashion collection. The Settling Rooms, the Indian Summer events, the regular Charter and Farmers markets in The Square and the town's festival calendar carry visitors through the year in south Leicestershire.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, inn and guesthouse trade serving the Harborough and Welland Valley visitor area, with a guide scene built on canal, Naseby battlefield and market-town tours. Market Harborough station runs direct trains to London St Pancras and Leicester on the Midland Main Line, while the A6 and A4304 carry day-trippers out from Kettering, Corby and Oadby across the season.

Garforth.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of east Leeds
s1loc: Garforth, the former Gascoigne colliery town east of Leeds first recorded as Gereford in the Domesday Book of 1086, anchors its visitor draw on Lotherton Hall nearby, the Edwardian estate of the Gascoigne family with its formal gardens, twelfth-century chapel and the Wildlife World zoo set in rolling countryside. The mining heritage told through the Garforth pits, the Isabella and Sisters shafts and the Barnbow story gives the area a genuine sense of place across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer spreads across the green spaces and trails around the town, with RSPB St Aidan's Nature Reserve at Swillington a marquee draw, a rewilded former opencast site of lakes and reedbed alongside the giant Oddball walking dragline excavator. Parlington Woods and the Dark Arch tunnel near Aberford, plus walking and cycling on the old Aberford Railway Fly Line trackbed, give families and activity operators a steady outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture run through Aberford close by, where the Gascoigne Almshouses, designed by George Fowler Jones and built in 1844 by the Gascoigne sisters in memory of their father Richard Oliver Gascoigne, line the old Great North Road. Becca Hall of 1783, the Parlington estate's Triumphal Arch and the historic coaching village on Ermine Street carry walkers and heritage visitors through the year on the eastern edge of Leeds.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving the Leeds and Wakefield visitor area, with a guide scene built on country-house, nature-reserve and mining-heritage tours. Garforth station runs direct trains to Leeds, York and Selby, while the A63, A642 and the M1 carry day-trippers out toward Lotherton, Temple Newsam and the towns of Leeds, Castleford and Pontefract across the season.

Droylsden.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Tameside
s1loc: Droylsden, the former mill town that grew along the Ashton Canal four miles east of Manchester, anchors its visitor draw on the Fairfield Moravian Settlement, the Grade I conservation village founded in 1785 with its Dutch-bell-towered church, square, schools and Georgian terraces, one of the most complete planned religious settlements in England. The Settlement and the wider Fairfield conservation area give the town a genuine heritage pull across the warmer season in Tameside.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Droylsden Marina, the waterside basin completed in 2012 at the junction of the Ashton Canal and the Hollinwood Branch, with towpath walking, cycling, canal boating and waterside cafes. The Medlock Valley trails, the green corridor toward Daisy Nook Country Park and the canal route on toward Portland Basin at Ashton give families and activity operators a steady outdoor offer through the season along the water.

Heritage and culture run through the industrial story of Fairfield Mills, where W. M. Christy and Sons wove the world's first machine-made terry towel in 1851, the Royal Turkish towels ordered by Queen Victoria herself. The Moravian church's archives and burial ground, the Christy towel heritage and the events around the Settlement and the Marina carry visitors through the year in this corner of Greater Manchester.

Underpinning it all is an inn and guesthouse trade serving the Tameside and east Manchester visitor area, with a guide scene built on canal, Moravian and industrial-heritage tours. The Droylsden and Audenshaw stops on the Manchester Metrolink Ashton line link the town to Manchester city centre and Ashton, while the A635 Manchester Road and the canal towpath carry day-trippers out from Ashton-under-Lyne, Denton and Stalybridge across the season.

Newquay.region: Newquay and the north Cornwall coast
Newquay.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the north Cornwall coast
s1loc: Newquay, Cornwall's surf capital, anchors its visitor economy on Fistral Beach, the Atlantic-facing strand that hosts international surfing competitions, with a string of golden beaches at Towan, Great Western, Tolcarne, Lusty Glaze, Porth and the Harbour drawing huge summer crowds. The Towan headland, the historic Huer's Hut and the famous suspension bridge to the island house above the bay give the resort a marquee seaside pull across the warmer season on the north coast.

The leisure and activity layer is built on the water, with surf schools, coasteering, kayaking and stand-up paddleboarding off Fistral and the harbour, plus the South West Coast Path striking out along the cliffs. The Blue Reef Aquarium with its 250,000-litre coral-reef ocean tank, Newquay Zoo with its thirteen-acre landscaped park, lions, lemurs and Humboldt penguins, and the Dragon Maze keep families and activity operators working hard through the season.

Heritage and culture run through Trenance Gardens and the boating lake, the Victorian Trenance Viaduct, and Trerice, the National Trust's Elizabethan manor just inland with its great hall and barn. The harbour's pilchard-fishing past, the Newquay carnival and Boardmasters surf and music festival on the cliffs above Watergate Bay carry visitors through the year on this stretch of the Cornish coast.

Underpinning it all is one of Cornwall's deepest hotel, holiday-park and guesthouse trades, with a wide surf-school and tour scene serving the coast. Newquay Airport runs flights across the country, the Atlantic Coast Line railway links Newquay to Par and the main line, and the A392 and A30 carry day-trippers out toward Watergate Bay, Holywell and the towns of Truro, St Austell and Bodmin across the season.

Truro.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Cornwall's cathedral city
s1loc: Truro, Cornwall's only city and its administrative heart, anchors its visitor economy on Truro Cathedral, the Gothic Revival masterpiece built between 1880 and 1910 and one of only three cathedrals in the country with three spires, towering over the Georgian streets below. The cathedral roof tours, the cobbled lanes and the elegant townhouses give the compact city a marquee heritage draw across the warmer season at the head of the Truro and Fal rivers.

The leisure and activity layer runs down to the water at Lemon Quay, the open events space with its weekly markets and the fifteen-foot bronze Drummer sculpture by Tim Shaw, and on to the Truro River, where boat trips run downstream to the Fal estuary and St Mawes. Boscawen Park, Victoria Gardens, Idless Woods and the surrounding creeks and countryside give families and activity operators a steady outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Royal Cornwall Museum, established in 1818 and the finest in the county, with its Mineral, Nature, Art and Ancient Civilisations galleries and over a million artefacts, and the Hall for Cornwall, the renovated theatre on Back Quay hosting West End shows and concerts. Lemon Street, one of the finest Georgian streets in the country, the Pannier Market and the city's festival calendar carry visitors through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, inn and guesthouse trade serving the central Cornwall visitor area, with a guide scene built on cathedral, river and Georgian-city tours. Truro station on the Cornish Main Line runs direct trains to London Paddington and Penzance, with the branch line to Falmouth, while the A39 and A390 carry day-trippers out toward Trelissick, the Roseland and the towns of Falmouth, Newquay and St Austell across the season.
